unit.title: Operate computer aided design (CAD) to produce basic drawing elements

summary: This unit teaches you to use a computer aided design (CAD) program to make accurate, basic drawings of steel parts. You will learn to set up a safe workstation and a new drawing, enter points with coordinates and object snaps, draw and edit lines, circles and shapes, organise your work on layers, add text and dimensions, and save, manage and print your drawings to scale.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It teaches you to use a **computer aided design (CAD)** program to produce the basic elements of an engineering drawing: lines, circles, arcs and shapes, placed exactly where they belong, on the right layers, with text and dimensions, saved safely and printed to scale.

CAD (also called computer aided drafting) is now the normal way to make fabrication drawings. Base plates, brackets, gates, grills, handrails, frames and tank stands are drawn on screen, printed for the shop floor, emailed to customers as PDF files and, in many shops, sent straight to a CNC plasma or laser cutting table. An accurate CAD drawing means accurate parts, less waste and fewer mistakes on the job.

**Who it is for:** welding trainees who can already read simple drawings (views, line types and dimensions). You do not need to have used CAD before, but you need basic computer skills: using a mouse and keyboard, and opening and saving files.

blocks.note: CAD programs differ in their menus, icons and some command names. The commands in this kit (Line, Circle, Offset, Trim, Fillet, Array and so on) are found in almost every 2D CAD program, and the typed forms shown (such as @50,0) are the ones most programs use. Your instructor will show you where each one is in the Centre's program: check yours.
blocks.label: Remember

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at the CAD workstation
rows: Set up the chair, desk and screen to avoid strain; take breaks; keep cables, plugs and drinks safe.
Start from the template; set millimetre units; check the layers, text style, dimension style and title block; save the file at once.
Use absolute, relative and polar coordinates, the drawing aids (grid, snap, ortho) and object snaps, never guessing by eye.
Draw lines, polylines, rectangles, circles, arcs, polygons and hatching, and use blocks for repeated items.
Use erase, move, copy, rotate, scale, mirror, offset, trim, extend, fillet, chamfer, array, stretch and explode.
Put outlines, hidden lines, centre lines, dimensions and text on their own layers with the right linetype and lineweight.
Add clear notes and correct dimensions of the right type, and fill in the title block.
Measure distances and areas with the inquiry tools and compare them with the sketch before you print.
Name, file, back up and revise drawings so that nothing is lost and the right version is always used.
Set the printer, paper, area and a stated scale, preview, print, and measure the print to prove the scale.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on workstation safety, set-up, coordinates, drawing aids, draw and edit commands, layers, text, dimensions, files and printing.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact command names and terms) and longer answers in full sentences, such as how to set up a drawing or how to print to scale.

**Practical tasks** at a CAD workstation: drawing and dimensioning a plate with holes using coordinates, layers and editing commands, and producing a two-view drawing with a title block, printed to scale. The assessor also watches your posture, your saving and your file names.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact words such as origin, relative, model space, explode, rotate, snap, intersection, text style and A3. Learn the key terms in the Revision section.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: CAD work means long hours at a screen, with your eyes fixed on small details and one hand on the mouse. The main risks are **eye strain**, **pain in the neck, back and shoulders**, **pain in the wrists and hands** from repeated small movements, and **electrical and tripping hazards** from cables and plugs. Set up the workstation before you start, not after it hurts.

head: Part
Set it up like this
Why
rows: Height set so your feet are flat on the floor (or on a footrest) and your knees are about level with your hips
Sit right back so the backrest supports your lower back
Supports your back and stops you leaning forward for hours
Forearms about level with the desk, elbows close to your sides, shoulders relaxed
Wrists straight, not bent up or resting on a hard edge
Mouse right beside the keyboard, at the same height
Stops strain in the shoulders, forearms and wrists
Straight in front of you, about an arm's length away
Top of the screen at or a little below eye level
Keeps your neck straight and your eyes looking slightly down, which is restful
Screen side-on to windows, not facing them or with a window behind it
Blinds closed when the sun shines on the screen
Brightness to suit the room; text big enough to read without leaning in
Glare and reflections make you squint and strain your eyes
Raise the screen on a stand or a firm box
Use a separate keyboard and mouse for long sessions
A laptop on a desk makes you bend your neck down for hours

blocks.h: Breaks and rest for your eyes

ul: Take a short break of about **5 to 10 minutes every hour**: stand up, walk, stretch your neck, shoulders and hands.
Every 20 minutes or so, look at something far away (about 6 metres) for about 20 seconds. This lets your eye muscles relax.
Blink often. People blink less when they stare at a screen, which dries the eyes.
Keep the screen clean, and tell your instructor if you get headaches, blurred vision or pain that does not go away after rest.
Check the plug, cable and power strip before you start. Do not use anything cracked, burnt or with bare wires: report it and tag it DO NOT USE.
Do not overload a power strip, and never plug one power strip into another.
Keep drinks and food away from the computer. A spill can wreck the keyboard or the computer and can cause a shock.
Keep cables tidy and out of walkways, so that no one trips or pulls a computer off the desk.
Never open the computer case or the printer's covers beyond what the maker's instructions allow. Report faults to your instructor.

blocks.note: Power cuts and voltage surges, especially in thunderstorms, can damage computers and wipe out unsaved work. Use the surge protector or UPS (uninterruptible power supply) the Centre provides, turn on your program's automatic save, and press Save every 10 to 15 minutes.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Pain, tingling or numbness in the hands, wrists, neck or back that comes back each time you work is a warning. Tell your instructor early: a small change to the chair, screen or mouse now prevents a long-term injury.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: CAD basics: the screen, commands and views

head: Point
CAD
Drawing by hand
rows: Sizes are typed in and points are picked with object snaps, so lines are exact
Depends on the skill of the person, the pencil and the scale rule
Move, stretch, trim or add a hole in seconds, without redrawing
Rub out, or redraw the whole sheet
Copy, array or insert a block (a title block, bolt holes, a standard part)
Every item is drawn again by hand
Print at any scale, any number of times; send a PDF by email; send outlines to a CNC cutting table
One original; photocopies; handed over or posted
Files take no space and can be backed up, but can be lost if they are not
Paper takes space and can tear, fade or get wet
Needs a computer, a program, electricity and training
Cheap; needs no power; works anywhere, even on site
Finished, accurate drawings, repeat work and drawings that will change
Quick sketches, ideas on site, and learning the rules of drawing

head: Part of the screen
What it does
rows: Where you draw. In **model space** you draw the part at full size.
Shows where you are pointing; a small box on it is used to pick objects.
Icons and menus for the commands.
Where you can type commands and values, and where the program tells you what it wants next (the **prompt**). Read it all the time.
Buttons to turn the drawing aids on and off (grid, snap, ortho, polar tracking, object snap), and the X and Y position of the cursor.
Sheets of paper set up for printing, with a border, a title block and windows (viewports) onto the model. This is often called **paper space**.
Shows which way the X and Y axes point.
Show and change the layer, colour, linetype and lineweight of objects.

ul: Start a command by clicking its icon, choosing it from a menu, or typing its name (or a short form, such as L for Line or C for Circle in many programs) and pressing **Enter**.
Then **read the prompt** on the command line and answer it: pick a point, type a value, or choose an option.
Press **Enter** to finish a command such as Line. In many programs, pressing Enter (or the space bar) again repeats the last command.
Press **Esc** to cancel a command you started by mistake.
Use **Undo** (often Ctrl + Z) to reverse the last action, and Redo to bring it back.
A right-click usually shows a short menu of options for the command you are in.

blocks.p: **Zoom** makes the drawing look bigger or smaller on the screen; **Pan** slides your view across the drawing. Neither changes the real size or position of anything. In many programs, rolling the mouse wheel zooms in and out at the cursor, and holding the wheel down while you move the mouse pans.

head: Zoom option
What it shows
rows: The area inside a box you drag round it
Everything that is drawn, as large as will fit on screen
The whole drawing area (the limits) or everything drawn, whichever is bigger
The view you had just before

blocks.note: Zoom and Pan change only your **view**. Move and Scale change the **objects** themselves. If a part has "disappeared", try Zoom Extents before you assume it is lost.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A few minutes of set-up saves hours later. The easiest way is to start from the Centre's **template file**: a starting drawing that already has the units, layers, text and dimension styles, and the title block. Check each setting anyway.

flow: Start a new drawing from the Centre's template
Check the units: millimetres, with the decimal places to suit the job (often 0 or 0.0), and angles in decimal degrees
Set the drawing limits or work area to fit the part at full size; turn on the grid and snap at a useful spacing, such as 10 mm
Check or create the layers you need
Check the text style and the dimension style
Save the file straight away, with a clear name, in the right folder
Fill in the title block (often on the layout), then start drawing

blocks.p: In model space, one drawing unit is one millimetre and you always draw the part at **full size (1:1)**. A gate 2,400 mm wide is drawn 2,400 units wide, even though it will be printed much smaller. The scale is chosen only when you print, or when you set up a viewport on a layout. Drawing at full size means every dimension measures the real size, and the distance and area tools give real answers.

blocks.note: Steel in Jamaica is often sold and talked about in inches and feet ("1-inch square tube", "a 10-foot gate"), and customers often measure in feet. Convert to millimetres before you draw: inches × 25.4, feet × 304.8. Write the conversion on the sketch so it can be checked.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: **Model space** is where you draw the part at full size.
A **layout** (paper space) is a sheet of paper of a set size, with a border and title block, and one or more **viewports**: windows that show the model at a set scale, such as 1:5.
For simple work you can print straight from model space at a stated scale. For finished drawings, many offices print from a layout. Follow the way the Centre's template is set up.

head: Aid
What it does
Use it when
rows: Shows a pattern of dots or lines at a set spacing. It does not print.
You want to judge sizes and positions roughly
Makes the cursor move only in set steps, such as every 10 mm
Points fall on a regular spacing
Keeps lines and movements horizontal or vertical only
Drawing square outlines, frames and bars
Shows guide lines at set angles, such as every 15° or 45°
Picks exact points on objects: ends, middles, centres, crossings
Always, when a point must touch something already drawn

blocks.note: Look at the status bar before you pick points, to see which aids are on. In many programs they are switched with buttons or function keys (for example F8 for Ortho). A grid snap left on by mistake makes the cursor jump past the point you want; turn it off when you are working with object snaps on odd sizes.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Layers work like clear sheets laid on top of each other. Every object sits on one layer, and each layer has its own **colour**, **linetype** and **lineweight**. Leave each object's own settings as **ByLayer**, so that it takes them from its layer. Then the lines look right on screen and print right, and you can control whole groups of objects at once.

head: Layer setting
What it does
rows: The layer that new objects are drawn on. Check it before you draw.
Off hides the layer's objects; they stay in the drawing and come back when it is turned on.
Frozen layers are hidden and ignored by the program, which can speed up a big drawing. The current layer cannot be frozen.
A locked layer's objects can be seen (and snapped to) but not changed. Useful for a title block or a finished outline.
The colour on screen; it can also control how the line prints.
Continuous, dashed (hidden), chain (centre) and so on.
How thick the line prints: thick for outlines, thin for the rest.

head: Suggested layer
Linetype
Lineweight (typical)
Used for
rows: Edges you cannot see from that view
Centre lines of holes, arcs and symmetrical parts
Temporary guide lines: turned off or frozen before printing
Border and title block: kept locked

blocks.note: Thick lines are usually about twice as thick as thin ones (for example 0.5 mm and 0.25 mm, or 0.7 mm and 0.35 mm). If a hidden or centre line shows as a solid line, its **linetype scale** does not suit the size of the drawing: change the linetype scale, not the layer. Use the layer names in the Centre's template if they differ from these.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Entering points: coordinates and object snaps

blocks.p: CAD places every point by its **coordinates**. The **X axis** runs across the screen and X gets bigger to the right. The **Y axis** runs up the screen and Y gets bigger upwards. The point where X and Y are both zero, 0,0, is the **origin**. A point is written X first, then Y, with a comma between: 50,20 means 50 mm to the right of the origin and 20 mm up.

head: Method
What you type (most programs)
Measured from
Example
rows: Start at 10,10, then type 90,10: the line ends 80 mm to the right, at 90,10
From 90,10, type @0,45: the line goes 45 mm straight up and ends at 90,55
Type @60<45: a 60 mm line going up and to the right at 45°
Point the cursor the way you want (with Ortho or polar tracking on) and type a length
The last point, in the cursor's direction
With Ortho on, point to the right and type 120: a 120 mm line to the right

blocks.p: Negative values go the other way: @-40,0 goes 40 mm to the **left**, and @0,-25 goes 25 mm **down**.
Angles are measured from the **3 o'clock direction** (along positive X, often called east), going **anticlockwise**. A negative angle goes clockwise.
An L-shaped plate is 80 mm across the bottom and 60 mm high, and both legs are 20 mm wide. Start the Line command at the origin and use relative coordinates all the way round.

blocks.note: Before you type, sketch the shape and write the length and direction of each side on it. Every relative move is "how far across, how far up" from where you are now, so add up the X moves and the Y moves round a closed shape: they must come back to zero.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Object snaps** make the cursor lock on to an exact point of an object that is already drawn. A marker of a different shape shows which snap has been found. Use them every time a point must touch, start from or line up with something.

head: Object snap
What it picks
Typical use
rows: The nearer end of a line or arc
The exact middle of a line or arc
The centre of a circle or arc
Hole centres; the centre of a polar array
The 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° points on a circle
Lines to the top, bottom or side of a circle
The point where two objects cross
Where centre lines cross, to place a hole
The point that makes a right angle with an object
A line square to another line
The point where a line just touches a circle or arc without cutting it
Lines joining two circles, as on a link plate
Any point on the object, close to the cursor
When a point must lie on an object, but not at a set place

ul: **Running** object snaps stay on all the time. Turn on only the few you use most (often Endpoint, Midpoint, Centre and Intersection), or the cursor will keep jumping to the wrong one.
A **one-off** snap (an override) works for one pick only. Choose it from the snap menu or type its short name when the program asks for a point.
If the wrong snap is found, zoom in so the objects are further apart, or use a one-off snap.

blocks.note: Never pick a point "by eye" where it should touch something. A line that looks joined on screen may miss by a fraction of a millimetre, and then Trim, Fillet, Hatch and the area tool will not work properly.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Command
What it draws
How it is usually set
rows: Straight lines; each segment is a separate object
Pick or type each point; Enter to finish; C to close
Joined lines and arcs that act as **one object**
Like Line, with options for arcs and width. A closed polyline is easy to offset and to measure for area.
Pick two opposite corners, for example 0,0 then @150,80
Centre and radius; centre and diameter; 2 points (the ends of a diameter); 3 points; or tangent, tangent, radius
Three points, or start, centre and end, and other options. Many programs draw arcs anticlockwise from the start point.
A regular shape with equal sides, such as a hexagon
Number of sides, centre, then inscribed or circumscribed and a radius
The ends of one axis and the half-length of the other
A pattern filling a closed area, such as a cut surface in a section view
Pick a point inside a closed boundary, or select the boundary; choose the pattern, angle and scale
A single line of text, or a paragraph (multiline) text box

ul: Drawings give holes by their **diameter**, with the sign Ø: Ø14 means a hole 14 mm across.
If the program asks for a radius, type **half the diameter**: Ø14 is radius 7. Many programs let you choose the Diameter option instead.
Place hole centres with coordinates, or with the Intersection snap where two centre lines cross.
**Tangent, tangent, radius** draws a circle of a set radius that just touches two lines or circles, for example a rounded end between two edges.

blocks.h: Polygons: hexagons for nuts and bars

blocks.p: Hexagons are given either **across flats** (AF: from one flat side to the opposite one, which is the spanner size) or across corners. The Polygon command lets you choose:

head: Option
The circle you give
Use it when the drawing gives
rows: The corners lie on the circle
The across-corners size: radius = half the across-corners size
The flat sides touch the circle
The across-flats size: radius = half the across-flats size

blocks.p: For example, a hexagon 24 mm across flats is a polygon with 6 sides, **circumscribed**, radius 12.

ul: Hatching shows a cut surface in a section view. A common pattern for steel is thin lines at 45°.
The boundary must be **completely closed**. A tiny gap, where lines do not quite meet, stops the hatch or makes it spill out over the drawing.
To find a gap, zoom in on the corners. Close it with Endpoint snaps, Extend, Fillet with radius 0, or by redrawing the outline as one closed polyline.
Set the hatch scale so the lines are evenly spaced on the printed sheet: neither a solid black mass nor lines so far apart they look like a mistake.

blocks.p: A **block** is a group of objects saved as one named item that you can insert again and again: a title block, a bolt, a standard bracket, a weld symbol. Every copy of a block is one object, which keeps the file small and tidy. If you change the block's definition, every copy in the drawing changes. **Explode** breaks a block (or a polyline or rectangle) back into separate simple objects, for example so that one line of it can be edited.

ul: Set up a **text style** first: the saved set of settings for the font and height. Use a plain, clear font.
Text heights are sizes on the **printed sheet**: about **3.5 mm** for notes and dimensions, 5 to 7 mm for titles, and never below about 2.5 mm.
Use single-line text for short labels and multiline (paragraph) text for notes of several lines.
Put all text on the Text layer, keep notes clear of the views, and write them in capitals if that is the Centre's practice.

blocks.note: If you print from a layout, the viewport's scale looks after text size. If you print straight from model space at 1:10, everything is printed ten times smaller, so text must be drawn ten times taller: 35 mm in the model gives 3.5 mm on paper. Some programs do this for you with an annotation scale. Ask your instructor which way the Centre works.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Most of the time spent on a CAD drawing is editing: tidying, copying and changing what is already there. Most editing commands first ask you to **select objects**, then press Enter, then answer the prompts.

head: Way to select
What it picks
rows: Window (in most programs, drag from **left to right**; the box has a solid edge)
Only objects that are **fully inside** the box
Crossing (in most programs, drag from **right to left**; the box has a dashed edge)
Every object that is inside the box **or touches** its edge
Removes an object from the selection

head: Command
What it does
What it usually asks for
rows: Select the objects, then Enter (the Delete key also works)
Moves objects to a new place
Objects, a base point, then the second point (or a distance)
Objects, a base point, then one or more second points
Turns objects about a base point; a positive angle turns them anticlockwise
Makes objects bigger or smaller about a base point: factor 2 doubles, 0.5 halves
Makes a reversed copy about a mirror line, like a reflection
Objects, two points on the mirror line, and whether to delete the original
Makes a parallel copy at an exact distance: a line beside a line, a bigger or smaller circle round the same centre
Distance, the object, then the side to offset to
Cuts off the part of an object that runs past a cutting edge
The cutting edges (or all objects), then the parts to cut off
Lengthens an object so that it meets a boundary
The boundary (or all objects), then the end to extend
Joins two objects with an arc of a set radius; with radius 0 it makes a clean, sharp corner
Cuts a corner with a straight, angled line at set distances (for example 5 mm × 5 mm)
Makes many evenly spaced copies: **rectangular** (rows and columns) or **polar** (round a centre)
Rectangular: rows, columns and spacing. Polar: centre, number of items, angle to fill
Moves part of a drawing and stretches the lines joined to it
A crossing box round the part to move, base point, second point
Cuts a gap in an object, or splits it at a point
The object and the break points
Joins lines or arcs that meet end to end into one object
Breaks a polyline, rectangle or block into simple separate objects

blocks.note: In a **rectangular array**, the spacing is from centre to centre (or from any point on one copy to the same point on the next), not the gap between the items. In a **polar array** of n items over 360°, the copies are 360 ÷ n degrees apart: 4 items are 90° apart, 6 are 60° apart, 8 are 45° apart.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Worked example: a base plate with holes

blocks.p: A base plate is 200 mm × 120 mm with 15 mm radius corners, four Ø16 holes 25 mm in from both edges, and a Ø50 hole in the middle. Put the bottom-left corner at the origin.

flow: Make Outline the current layer. Rectangle: first corner 0,0, other corner @200,120
Fillet: set the radius to 15, then pick the two sides at each corner (or use the polyline option to do all four at once)
Work out the hole centres: 25,25 and 175,25 along the bottom, 25,95 and 175,95 along the top (200 − 25 = 175; 120 − 25 = 95)
Circle at 25,25 with radius 8 (half of Ø16)
Rectangular array of that circle: 2 rows and 2 columns, row spacing 70 (95 − 25) and column spacing 150 (175 − 25). Or copy it with object snaps
Centre hole: circle at 100,60 (the middle of 200 × 120) with radius 25
Change to the Centre layer and add centre lines through each hole, running a little past the hole
Check sizes with the distance tool, then dimension on the Dimensions layer and save

blocks.note: Draw construction lines on a Construction layer when you need guides, for example lines 25 mm in from each edge made with Offset. Their crossings give the hole centres with the Intersection snap. Freeze or erase them before printing.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Turning a rough outline into a finished one

ul: Lines that cross at a corner: **Trim** each back to the other, or **Fillet with radius 0**.
A line that stops short of another: **Extend** it to meet the boundary.
An inside edge a set distance in from the outside: **Offset** the outline.
Rounded or bevelled corners: **Fillet** (arc) or **Chamfer** (angled cut).
A symmetrical part: draw half, then **Mirror** it.
Leftover guide lines: **Erase** them.
Finally, measure with the distance tool and compare with the sketch.

sections.title: Views, dimensions, title block and checking

blocks.p: One view rarely shows a part fully. A fabrication drawing usually has a **front view** and an **end view** or a **plan**, drawn **lined up** with each other so that every edge can be followed from one view to the next.

flow: Draw the front view first, on the Outline layer
With Ortho on, draw construction lines across from the top and bottom edges of the front view (and from any holes or steps)
Draw the end view between those lines, so that its heights match the front view exactly
Add hidden lines (Hidden layer) for edges that cannot be seen, and centre lines (Centre layer) for holes
Erase or freeze the construction lines, then dimension each view

ul: Edges you cannot see from a view are drawn as **hidden (dashed) lines**. For example, a hole through a plate seen from the edge shows as two hidden lines with a centre line between them.

The title block shows which **projection** is used, with its symbol. In first-angle projection, the view seen from the left is placed on the right of the front view; in third-angle projection, it is placed on the left. Use the projection the Centre uses.

blocks.p: Dimensions in CAD measure the objects themselves, so the part must be drawn accurately at full size first. Set the Dimensions layer current, and use a **dimension style** with the right text height (about 3.5 mm on the printed sheet), arrow size and units (millimetres).

head: Dimension type
Use it for
Example
rows: A sloping edge, measured along its true length
A brace cut at an angle
A note pointing to a feature
Several sizes from one datum edge, or in a chain
Hole positions from the left edge

ul: Pick the points with **object snaps**, so the dimension measures the true size.
Place dimensions **outside** the views where you can, with smaller ones nearer the view and overall sizes outside them, so that lines do not cross.
Give each size **once only**, and show hole positions from a **datum** (a chosen reference edge) to the hole centres.
Keep dimensions **associative**: an associative dimension is linked to the object and updates itself if the object is changed.
Never type over a dimension's number to "correct" it. If a dimension shows the wrong value, **the object is drawn wrong**: fix the object.

blocks.p: Add general notes on the Text layer, for example: ALL DIMENSIONS IN MM; MATERIAL: 6 MM MILD STEEL PLATE; GENERAL TOLERANCE ±1 MM UNLESS STATED; REMOVE ALL SHARP EDGES; and any welding notes. Check the spelling.

head: Item
Why it is needed
rows: Title of the part, and the drawing number
Says what the drawing is and lets it be found
Name (drawn by), checked by, and the date
Shows who is responsible and when it was made
Must match the scale the drawing is printed at
So the part is made from the right stock and sizes are not misread
So the right sheet and the latest version are used
Shows where the drawing came from

head: Tool
What it tells you
rows: The distance between two points you pick, with the angle and the X and Y differences
The area enclosed by a closed shape (in mm² when you draw in mm), and its perimeter
Details of an object: its layer, length, radius, position and so on
The X,Y coordinates of a point you pick

blocks.note: Area × thickness × 7850 kg/m³ gives the mass of a steel plate. A 200 mm × 120 mm plate is 24,000 mm², which is 0.024 m². At 6 mm (0.006 m) thick it weighs about 0.024 × 0.006 × 7850 ≈ 1.13 kg, a little less once the holes are cut. Handy for costing and lifting.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Before printing, check: the sizes match the sketch; every object is on the right layer; corners meet exactly; the dimensions and notes are correct; the title block is filled in; the construction layer is off.
Ask a classmate to check your sizes with the distance tool. A second pair of eyes finds mistakes you no longer see.

head: Command
What it does
rows: Writes your changes into the **same file**, with the same name and in the same place
Saves a **copy with a new name or in a new place**; from then on you are working in the new file and the old one stays as it was

ul: Save the drawing **as soon as you start it**, with its proper name, then save often (every 10 to 15 minutes) and always before printing.
Turn on the program's automatic save, but do not rely on it alone.
Use Save As to start a new version, so that an approved drawing is never written over by mistake.
Give every file a name that says what it is: the **job number, the part name and the drawing number**, for example J215-gate-frame-D02. Never leave the name the program gives (Drawing1).
Keep files in folders: one for each job or customer, in the **shared folder** the Centre uses, not on the desktop of one computer.
Do not save over another person's drawing. If you need to change it, ask, then use Save As with your initials or a new revision.

head: File type
What it is for
rows: The program's own drawing file (in many programs, .dwg)
A starting file with units, layers, styles and the title block set up
A common exchange format that most other CAD programs and CNC plasma and laser cutting tables can read
For people who need to view or print the drawing without CAD, such as customers and the shop floor
An automatic copy of the version before your last save, which can be renamed and opened if the main file is damaged

blocks.p: A file can be deleted, written over, damaged by a power cut or lost with a stolen or broken computer. Keep a **backup** in another place: the Centre's backup or network drive, cloud storage, or a memory stick kept apart from the computer. Update it at the end of every session. A backup on the same computer is lost with that computer.
Once a drawing has been issued (given to the shop floor or the customer), it is never quietly changed. If it must change:

flow: Save As a new file for the new revision, so the issued revision is kept
Make the change
Change the revision letter, for example from A to B
Write in the revision table what was changed, the date and your initials
Issue the new revision, and take back or mark old prints SUPERSEDED so no one works from them
Save the drawing
Open the print (plot) settings, or the layout set up for printing
Choose the printer, or a PDF printer to make a PDF file
Choose the paper size (such as A4 or A3) and the direction (landscape or portrait)
Choose what to print: the layout, the extents of the drawing, or a window round the border
Set a stated scale, such as 1:1, 1:5 or 1:10, **not fit to paper**
Set the lines to print black, with thick and thin lineweights; centre the print on the paper
Use print preview to check that everything fits inside the border and can be read
Print, then measure a known dimension on the paper with a rule to prove the scale

blocks.p: Each A size is half of the one above it. Most school and workshop printers take A4 and A3.
A scale of **1:n** means that 1 mm on the paper stands for n mm on the real part. Divide the real size by n to find the printed size; multiply a measured size by n to find the real size.

head: Scale
Meaning
A real length of 1,000 mm prints as

blocks.p: To choose a scale, divide the largest size of the part by the space on the sheet, and take the next standard scale. For example, a frame 1,600 mm long on an A3 sheet with about 380 mm of drawing space: 1:2 gives 800 mm (too big), 1:5 gives 320 mm (fits, with room for dimensions).

blocks.note: **Fit to paper** prints at whatever odd scale fills the sheet, such as 1:7.38. Nobody can measure from it, and the scale in the title block is then wrong. The same happens when a PDF is printed with "Fit" ticked: print PDF drawings at **actual size (100%)**.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Keep your fingers out of the printer while it runs. The inside of a laser printer gets very hot. Clear paper jams only as the maker's instructions say, and report faults.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it at the workstation.

ul: I can set up a CAD workstation to avoid eye strain and pain in my neck, back and wrists, and work safely with cables, plugs and drinks.
I can explain why I take short breaks and how I rest my eyes.
I can name the parts of the CAD screen and start, finish, cancel and undo commands.
I can explain the difference between Zoom and Pan, and Move and Scale.
I can start a drawing from a template, set millimetre units and draw at full size.
I can convert metres, inches and feet to millimetres.
I can use the grid, snap, ortho, polar tracking and object snaps.
I can enter points with absolute, relative and polar coordinates, and say which way any angle points.
I can draw lines, polylines, rectangles, circles, arcs, polygons and hatching, and use blocks.
I can select objects with a window and with a crossing box.
I can use erase, move, copy, rotate, scale, mirror, offset, trim, extend, fillet, chamfer, array, stretch and explode.
I can set up and use layers with the right linetypes and lineweights, and turn layers off, freeze and lock them.
I can draw two views lined up with each other, with hidden lines and centre lines.
I can add text and the right types of dimension, and fill in a title block.
I can check sizes and areas with the inquiry tools.
I can name, save, back up and revise drawing files correctly.
I can print a drawing to a stated scale and check the scale on the paper.

terms: Points measured from the origin, typed as X,Y
A dimension that measures a sloping edge along its true length
Evenly spaced copies in rows and columns (rectangular) or round a centre (polar)
A dimension that updates itself when the object it measures changes
A group of objects saved as one named item that can be inserted many times
Computer aided design (or drafting): making drawings on a computer
Where commands and values are typed and the program's prompts appear
A selection box that picks everything inside it or touching it
Breaks a block, polyline or rectangle into separate simple objects
Lengthens an object to meet a boundary
Joins two objects with an arc of a set radius; radius 0 gives a sharp corner
A pattern of dots or lines on screen that helps you judge sizes; it does not print
A pattern filling a closed area, used to show cut surfaces
A named group of objects with its own colour, linetype and lineweight
A sheet set up for printing, with a title block and viewports
The pattern of a line: continuous, dashed (hidden) or chain (centre)
The drawing area where the part is drawn at full size
A tool that picks an exact point on an object, such as an endpoint or centre
A parallel copy at an exact distance
The point 0,0, where X and Y are both zero
A mode that keeps lines horizontal or vertical
Slides the view across the drawing without changing the zoom or the objects
A distance and an angle from the last point, typed as @distance<angle
Joined lines and arcs that act as one object
Points measured from the last point, typed with @
A new issue of a drawing after a change, shown by a new letter and a note in the revision table
The ratio of the printed size to the real size, such as 1:5
A mode that makes the cursor move in set steps
A starting file with units, layers, styles and title block already set up
The saved settings for text font and height
The box on a drawing giving its title, number, scale, projection, material, name and date
Cuts off the part of an object that runs past a cutting edge
Changes how big the drawing looks on screen, not its real size

c1.title: A pump base plate in Old Harbour
c1.text: Kerry-Ann is on work experience at a small fabrication shop in Old Harbour, St Catherine. She must draw a base plate for a water pump from the supervisor's sketch: 6 mm mild steel plate, 240 mm × 160 mm, with four Ø18 holes whose centres are 30 mm in from both edges. She puts the bottom-left corner of the plate at the origin, 0,0, and draws on the Centre's template.

c2.title: A driveway gate drawing in Ocho Rios
c2.text: Damion works for a gate and grill business in Ocho Rios, St Ann. He has drawn a driveway gate 3,000 mm wide and 1,500 mm high in model space at full size, and must print it on A3 paper, which leaves about 380 mm of width for the drawing inside the border. He will print straight from model space. Some of his centre lines were drawn on the Outline layer by mistake.

c3.title: A site office in Montego Bay
c3.text: Shawna-Kay draws handrail and staircase details on a laptop in a container office at a hotel building site in Montego Bay, St James. The laptop sits on a low table, the screen faces a bright window, and she has worked for two and a half hours without a break. Her neck aches and her eyes are sore. The laptop charger, a printer, a fan and a kettle are all plugged into one power strip, which is plugged into a second strip whose cable runs across the doorway.

c4.title: A changed bracket drawing in Kingston
c4.text: At a steel shop in Kingston, Jevaughn drew a pump bracket, saved it as J318-pump-bracket-A, and printed it for the shop floor as revision A. The customer now wants the holes changed from Ø14 to Ø16. Jevaughn's only copy of the file is on the desktop of the workshop computer. The customer also wants the bracket outline cut on a CNC plasma table at another firm.

c5.title: A tank outlet flange in May Pen
c5.text: Oshane, a trainee in May Pen, Clarendon, is drawing a round flange for a water tank outlet: Ø150 outside, a Ø60 hole in the middle, and six Ø14 bolt holes equally spaced on a 110 mm pitch circle diameter (PCD). He draws the Ø150 circle with its centre at 0,0, and plans to draw one bolt hole and then make the rest with a polar array.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann needs the centre of the hole nearest the top-right corner of the plate. What are its coordinates?
questions.why: The top-right corner is at 240,160, so a centre 30 mm in from both edges is at 240 − 30 = 210 across and 160 − 30 = 130 up. X is always written first.

questions.q: She draws the first hole at 30,30 and copies it with a rectangular array of 2 rows and 2 columns. Which spacings should she enter?
o: Rows 160 mm apart and columns 240 mm apart
Rows 100 mm apart and columns 180 mm apart
Rows 130 mm apart and columns 210 mm apart
Rows 30 mm apart and columns 30 mm apart
questions.why: Array spacing is centre to centre. The centres are 30 mm in from each edge, so they are 160 − 60 = 100 mm apart up the plate and 240 − 60 = 180 mm apart across it.

questions.q: The Circle command asks Kerry-Ann for a radius. What should she type for each hole?
questions.why: Ø18 is the diameter, so the radius is half of it: 9 mm. Typing 18 at the radius prompt would draw a Ø36 hole; many programs also offer a Diameter option.

questions.q: Her dimension across the plate shows 239.5 instead of 240. What should she do?
o: Fix the outline so it is drawn 240 mm wide
Type 240 over the number in the dimension
Leave it, as half a millimetre will not matter
Delete the dimension and write 240 as text
questions.why: A CAD dimension measures the object, so a wrong value means the outline is drawn wrong. Typing over the number hides the mistake, and the CNC or the shop floor would then work from a wrong drawing.

questions.q: Which standard scale is the largest that will fit the 3,000 mm gate into the 380 mm of space, with room left for dimensions?
questions.why: At 1:10 the gate prints 300 mm wide, leaving 80 mm for dimensions. At 1:5 it would be 600 mm, which does not fit; 1:20 fits but makes the drawing smaller than it needs to be.

questions.q: Damion's notes must be 3.5 mm high on the paper. How tall should he make the text in model space for a 1:10 print?
o: 3.5 mm, the same as on the paper
0.35 mm, a tenth of the paper size
35 mm, ten times the paper size
10 mm, the same as the scale number
questions.why: Printing from model space at 1:10 makes everything ten times smaller, so text must be drawn ten times taller to print at 3.5 mm. A layout viewport or an annotation scale can do this for you.

questions.q: His centre lines print as thick continuous lines. What is the best fix?
o: Make the centre lines' own colour red so they stand out
Move them onto the Centre layer, set to ByLayer
Turn the Outline layer off before he prints the drawing
Erase them and leave the centre lines off this drawing
questions.why: The Centre layer carries the chain linetype and thin lineweight, so objects on it set to ByLayer print correctly. Turning off Outline would hide the gate itself, and centre lines are needed to locate the bars and hinges.

questions.q: Damion measures the 3,000 mm width on his print and gets 287 mm instead of 300 mm. What is the most likely cause?
o: The layer lineweights were set too thin
The drawing was not saved before printing
The print was set to fit the paper
The grid was left switched on
questions.why: Fit to paper prints at an odd scale (here about 1:10.45) that matches no title block. Set a stated scale of 1:10 and measure again; lineweights, saving and the grid do not change printed sizes.

questions.q: Which change will do most to ease Shawna-Kay's aching neck?
o: Turn the screen brightness up so that she can see more clearly
Tilt the laptop screen further back on the low table
Pull her chair closer so that she can lean in to the screen
Raise the laptop on a stand, with a separate keyboard
questions.why: A laptop on a low table makes you bend your neck down for hours. Raising the screen to about eye level, and typing on a separate keyboard and mouse, keeps the neck straight.

questions.q: What should she do about the bright window?
o: Turn the table so the window is to one side
Sit so that the bright window is right behind the screen
Turn the screen brightness right down so the glare is less
Wear dark sunglasses while she works at the screen
questions.why: A window behind the screen makes you look into bright light, and a window behind you reflects off the screen. With the window to the side, and blinds closed in strong sun, glare is cut.

questions.q: What is the right action about the power strips and cable?
o: Tape the cable to the doorway floor and carry on as before
Unplug just the kettle, and leave everything else as it is
Use one strip, move the kettle, and reroute the cable
Switch the second strip off at night and use it by day
questions.why: One power strip plugged into another, with a kettle as well, can overload and overheat. The cable across the doorway is a trip hazard that could also pull the laptop off the table.

questions.q: What should Jevaughn do to make the hole change properly?
o: Change the holes and save over revision A, since it is still the same part
Make revision B, note the change and date, and recall the A prints
Give it a brand-new drawing number so that the old file is never touched
Mark the change in pen on the shop floor print and leave the file as it is
questions.why: An issued drawing keeps its history. The new revision letter and the note in the revision table show what changed and when, and recalling or marking the old prints stops anyone drilling Ø14 holes from revision A.

questions.q: Which action keeps the revision A file exactly as it was issued?
o: Pressing Save after each change he makes
Turning on the program's automatic save
Save As with a new name before any change
Closing the drawing without saving changes
questions.why: Save As makes a new file and leaves the old one untouched. Save writes the changes into the same file, so revision A would be lost; closing without saving loses the new work instead.

questions.q: Where is the best place for a backup of Jevaughn's drawings?
o: In a second folder on that computer's desktop
In the computer's recycle bin, to restore later
On the shared drive, away from that computer
Inside the same file, saved under the same name
questions.why: A backup must survive if this computer breaks, is stolen or catches a virus. A copy on the same computer is lost along with it.

questions.q: Which file type should he send so the other firm's CNC plasma table can cut the outline?
o: A PDF of the printed drawing
A DXF of the outline
A photo of the screen
A copy of the template file
questions.why: DXF is the common exchange format that most CAD programs and CNC cutting tables can read as real geometry. A PDF or photo is a picture to look at, not lines a machine can follow.

questions.q: Oshane draws the first bolt hole on the pitch circle, to the right of the flange centre (at 0°). Where is its centre?
questions.why: The pitch circle diameter is 110 mm, so its radius is 55 mm, and the point at 0° is 55 mm to the right of 0,0. 75 is the radius of the outside edge, and 0,55 is on the pitch circle but at 90°.

questions.q: He wants to draw the pitch circle with Offset from the Ø150 outline. What offset distance should he use?
o: 40 mm
55 mm
95 mm
20 mm
questions.why: Offset works on the radius: 150 ÷ 2 = 75 and 110 ÷ 2 = 55, so the pitch circle is 75 − 55 = 20 mm inside the outline. 40 mm is the difference in diameters.

questions.q: After the polar array of six holes over 360°, how far apart are the hole centres measured round the flange?
questions.why: A polar array spreads the items evenly: 360° ÷ 6 = 60°. Four holes would be 90° apart and eight would be 45° apart.

questions.q: Tajay drags a box from right to left across part of his drawing, and objects that only touch the box are picked as well. Why?
o: He was still in the middle of the Trim command
Right to left makes a crossing selection
Object snap was turned on when he dragged it
The objects are all on a layer that is locked
questions.why: In most programs, a box dragged right to left is a crossing selection: it picks anything inside it or touching it. Dragged left to right, it is a window that picks only objects fully inside.

questions.q: A customer's sketch gives a handrail as 8 feet long. With the units set to millimetres, what length should you draw?
questions.why: One foot is 304.8 mm, so 8 × 304.8 = 2,438.4 mm. 96 is the length in inches, and rounding to 2,400 would make the rail almost 40 mm short.
